title: I kept losing momentum on AI game projects, so I made myself 4 checklists to stop winging it
author: Trashy_io
selftext:
I am a pretty active member in this sub and love seeing everyones creativity shine through their projects, but I kept noticing in AI game dev was that it’s really easy to generate momentum early, then drift because nothing is clearly scoped, tracked, or exit-criteria’d.

So I made myself 4 simple docs to keep projects organized. To help keep me on track while giving myself everything I need to consider all in one place. Checklist/Outline are as follows

GDD Outline, Marketing Checklist, Release Checklist, and a Prototype Exit Checklist. 

They’re basically meant to answer:

“What am I building?”

“What does ‘good enough to move on’ look like?”

“What still needs to happen before I try to sell this?”

I originally made them for myself about a month ago because I was tired of bouncing between half-finished ideas and messy AI-assisted workflows.

If peps here think this would be useful, I can also post a free example section in the comments. I also bundled the full set on Gumroad and can link it there is any interest, but I mostly wanted to see whether this kind of resource is actually useful to other AI game devs.

It is priced at $3 but since this is the best community on reddit if you are interested in the docs but dont have the $3 to spare DM me and ill give them to you for free as I want everyone in this community to find success and a easier time doing so!

comments.author: certaintyisuncertain
comments.body:
I think “What still needs to happen before I try to sell this?” is important.

I really didn't think of that with the game I was working on, I just thought of a subscription based on the costs I'm incurring, but realized pretty quickly that isn't good enough. So I'm working on the couple of key features that I think will make it worth paying for.

replies.author: Trashy_io
replies.body:
I did the same thing with my project, just started building and realized I had no end goal in terms of monetizing or even a ending to the feature creep lol 

I think approaching projects from the start with a full-ish outline filled out is the key to actually finishing projects and staying organized. At least just enough to keep the project flowing forward in the right direction.

replies.author: certaintyisuncertain
replies.body: I do this with apps or features for my full-time job too. I keep a folder in my notes app that i just full of ideas. Otherwise they gnaw at me, but if I can just brain-dump the ideas, then they don't feel lost and I can focus on the ones that have the most progress or legs.

replies.author: Trashy_io
replies.body:
Thats a really good system as well I do the same on top of the docs. The docs are where the organized thoughts live, and the phones folders are where the chaos is rampant and embraced. 

I have a folder that goes down to the maxed out sub folder limit for game dev which I didn't even know was a thing lmao. But it is a way better system than like you said having ideas block focus or switch focus constantly

comments.author: MakkoMakkerton
comments.body: Is cool but the issue with AI games isn't how to build them its how to market them without getting labeled sloppy and hated by the general gaming community

replies.author: Trashy_io
replies.body:
Thats a fair point but I feel like that thought in the gaming space is slowly going away and will eventually become a super small group 
The only way to combat that is to add extra polish and creative intent behind our games. Its just whats popular to hate on right now just like bitcoin was or any new tech that has ever came along. 

And I sure wish I was buying bitcoin back in even 2016 rather than second guessing the tech. Which is smart to do but standing on the sidelines and just waiting for stuff to get figured out is how you get lose out on opportunities. And I am going to make the most use of this technology that I can as I have been patiently waiting for an opportunity like this for a while. The opportunity is being an early adopter and knowing the tech better than anyone else. 

Those are my thoughts on the overall stigma towards AI atm. I was on the other side not all that long ago. It wasn't until I started doing research and taking courses over AI that I had realized that this is a massive opportunities that can come with safely using AI and LLMs

replies.author: The-Eucharist
replies.body:
With all due respect, you're already way behind being an early adopter. 

A genuine question: What are you envisaging? A golden age where you type in your ideas and the game creates itself for you without any knowledge of coding?

Because by the time that is even slightly possible, the people with actual game design skill, the ability to pull it all together coherently and create immersive and popular games will be way ahead. 

No offence, they won't be knocking out dreadful knock off TD and Sudoku clones as per your itch.io

Here's a thought: invest in some hard work. I'm going to assume you're quite young - take some time to read / study / learn and practice game design theory. And also at least bang in some basic #C coding just so you can catch the mistakes.

Again, no offence but we're a world away from what you're thinking and your is best spent learning rather than waiting for AI to get where you want it to be
